result: In 80 post-COVID syndrome patients (40 meeting ME/CFS criteria) vs 38 seronegative and 40 asymptomatic post-COVID controls, several GPCR autoantibodies were lower, not higher, in PCS; ADRB2, STAB1 and ADRA2A antibodies were the strongest random-forest classifiers, and ADRB2 antibody levels correlated with fatigue and vasomotor severity in PCS/ME/CFS.
reason: Same GPCR autoantibody measure in a long COVID cohort, but it finds lower levels with severity correlations, so it does not replicate an elevation. Better read as a long COVID extension.

result: Retrospective comparison of 59 long COVID and 55 post-infectious ME/CFS patients found the same frequency of core symptoms and the same magnitude of exercise-induced rectus femoris M-wave alterations during and after cycling; M-wave changes were larger in ME/CFS at the highest strength and performance levels.
reason: Measures exercise-induced M-wave changes (membrane excitability), not myopathic needle EMG or biopsy, so it fits the M-wave finding and adds a long COVID version.

result: Phage-display profiling (244,000 microbiota and viral antigen variants) found severe ME/CFS patients had distinct, overrepresented serum antibody epitope repertoires against Lachnospiraceae flagellins, and machine-learning classifiers built on this antibody binding added diagnostic information beyond standard blood tests.
reason: Measures serum antibody reactivity to gut microbe antigens in severe ME/CFS, not LPS, LBP, sCD14 or anti-LPS translocation markers. Closest fit is the gut-microbe serum reactivity finding, although the direction there (reduced overall IgG) differs.

result: In 67 female ME/CFS patients and 48 matched controls, patients had higher resting BP and HR; the rest of the results (orthostatic wrist temperature, 24-h skin temperature rhythm, circulating endothelial biomarkers including endothelin-1) are cut off in the abstract.
reason: Does not measure FMD or PORH, and the truncated abstract gives no endothelial biomarker results to link elsewhere (vascular-vascular-proteins-blood would be the candidate if the full results were available).

result: Study protocol for a planned cross-sectional multimodal MRI study of neurovascular coupling (task-fMRI HRF, breath-hold RRF, functional MRS glutamate) in 288 participants; reports no results.
reason: Protocol with no measured results. It also does not concern conventional structural MRI.

result: 3-6 months after hospital discharge, 37 long COVID patients with severe fatigue showed raised monocyte inflammatory gene expression, raised serum IL-6, TNF-alpha, galectin-9 and CXCL10, and more CD8+ T cells than controls; non-fatigued long COVID subgroups (n=36) showed other T-cell and inflammatory patterns.
reason: Targeted monocyte gene expression and cytokine and flow data in hospitalised long COVID, not ME/CFS single-cell transcriptomics. Fits long COVID immune profiling, adding a fatigue-defined subgroup, and also raised galectin-9.

result: Non-invasive CPET in 120 symptomatic post-COVID patients who reached adequate exertion: 65% showed no limitation, 15.8% deconditioning, 9.2% pulmonary mechanical limitation (mostly dysfunctional breathing), 5.8% pulmonary vascular and 4.2% cardiac limitation.
reason: Non-invasive CPET with no oxygen-extraction or cardiac-output measurement, so not iCPET. It fits the long COVID CPET-pattern finding (deconditioning, no cardiac or ventilatory limit in most patients).

result: Among 634 German children and adolescents, clustered DSQ ME/CFS symptoms were reported by 40.0% of seropositive vs 29.6% of seronegative children; after adjustment the risk ratio fell from 1.35 to 1.18 (95% CI 0.90-1.53, not significant), although substantial fatigue stayed raised (aRR 2.08, 1.05-4.13).
reason: Tests whether SARS-CoV-2 infection raises ME/CFS risk and finds no significant adjusted excess in a paediatric cross-sectional sample, so it is a null result (with caveats: symptom questionnaire, not criteria) rather than an extension.

result: Whole-cell patch-clamp of NK cells (n=5 per group) showed PregS-induced TRPM3 currents reduced in ME/CFS (p=0.0048) and in post-COVID condition (p=0.0039) vs controls, with no difference between ME/CFS and post-COVID, and both patient groups resistant to ononetin.
reason: Same group and method (not independent replication). Its main contribution is the post-COVID version, so extends. The sample is tiny.

result: In Australian primary-care records (MedicineInsight, 2015-2019), crude ME/CFS prevalence among regularly attending patients aged 13 and over was 94.9-103.9 per 100,000 (about 0.1%), higher in females (130.0-141.4) than males (50.9-57.5), about 2.5:1, peaking at ages 40-59; qualitative data suggest underestimation.
reason: Recorded-diagnosis prevalence in a new country, below the 0.2-1% range and with a lower F:M ratio than 3-4x, so it adds a primary-care data point rather than replicating.
